clue.text: Dramatic line in discards

parts.note: an actor's line delivered casually, as if tossed aside with things got rid of

explanation.surface: A line of a play turns up among rejected papers.
explanation.walkthrough: An actor 'throws away' a line by saying it offhandedly; the same word describes things discarded.
explanation.definitionFit: A casually tossed-off line in a play is called by the same word as rubbish one discards.

clue.text: Digital sketch

parts.note: a small quick drawing, read also as something belonging to a finger or digit

explanation.surface: A sketch made on a computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' suggests computers, but it means 'of a digit': the horny plate on the thumb also names a tiny sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: A miniature quick drawing shares its name with the plate on a digit's tip.

clue.text: What every funambulist should know

parts.note: a tightrope walker literally needs to know the cords; the idiom means knowing how things work

explanation.surface: Advice for a tightrope walker.
explanation.walkthrough: A funambulist is a tightrope walker; 'to know the ropes' is to be experienced in a job.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines of cord are both a tightrope walker's footing and, in the idiom, the know-how of any trade.

clue.text: Authorizes hostile Gasconades

parts.note: war is the hostile state, as in a war footing
gasconades are boastful tirades, bombastic speeches

explanation.surface: Someone sanctions aggressive bragging.
explanation.walkthrough: Gasconade, from the boastful Gascons of France, is bragging talk, so rants.
explanation.definitionFit: Warrants as a verb means sanctions or justifies, giving official permission.

clue.text: Having done the dishes feeling a bit off

definitions.meaning: after cleaning the plates you have washed them up
informally, finished or worn out, past one's best

explanation.surface: Someone feels unwell after clearing up the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, having cleaned the crockery; figuratively, exhausted or done for.

clue.text: Salvation to the chap who's a beefeater

definitions.text: Salvation to the chap who's a beefeater

parts.words: Salvation to the chap who's a beefeater
parts.note: a beefeater is a Warder of the Tower of London, and to do this man's service is to save a situation

explanation.surface: A Tower of London guard is rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: Beefeaters are the Yeoman Warders of the Tower of London; 'yeoman service' is help given in a crisis, the salvation of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tower guards are Yeoman Warders, and the phrase 'yeoman service' means rescue in need.

clue.text: Equestrian corollary

definitions.meaning: a supplementary proposition or added clause following from another

explanation.surface: A horse-related consequence.
explanation.definitionFit: One who sits on a horse; also a clause or proposition added to a statement, as in geometry exercises.

clue.text: Nathaniel the sailor comes up for the cane

indicators.note: in a down entry coming up means the run of letters is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Nat is a short form of the name Nathaniel
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor called Nathaniel is summoned to be flogged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes up' turns NAT followed by TAR, giving NATTAR backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Rattan is the climbing palm whose stems are used for walking sticks and wicker.

clue.text: Poor dancers some of these brothers

definitions.text: Poor dancers some of these brothers

parts.words: Poor dancers some of these brothers
parts.note: members of a Muslim religious fraternity vowed to poverty, some of whom whirl in worship

explanation.surface: Some of these brothers dance badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor dancers' looks like a criticism, but it means mendicant (poor) men, some of whom are whirling dancers.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Sufi orders take vows of poverty, and some perform whirling dances as worship.

clue.text: Not that the Bishop encourages speeding through his see !

definitions.text: Not that the Bishop encourages speeding through his see !

parts.words: Not that the Bishop encourages speeding through his see !
parts.note: the cathedral city's name reads as an order to tear along at speed

explanation.surface: A bishop disapproves of fast drivers in his diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yorkshire cathedral city's name splits as 'rip on', an urging to speed; a bishop's see is his diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: The cathedral city is the seat of a bishop, whose name sounds like a cry to go faster.

clue.text: Men of decision in the field

definitions.text: Men of decision in the field

parts.words: Men of decision in the field
parts.note: officials on a playing field who give the rulings

explanation.surface: Decisive men out in the countryside or in action.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket and other sports officials make the decisions on the pitch.

clue.text: A rocky appearance, but not in hair-style

parts.note: out is the opposite of in, as of fashion
a crop is a short haircut

explanation.surface: A rugged look that is unfashionable as a haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'not in' as unfashionable, but it is simply OUT, followed by a CROP haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock that emerges at the surface of the ground is an exposure of bedrock.

clue.text: Arabs wandering in Iraq

indicators.note: letters that wander move about, so the word Arabs is rearranged

explanation.surface: Nomads roam across Iraq.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the place itself: a port city found in Iraq.
explanation.definitionFit: The port city on the Shatt al-Arab lies in the south of Iraq.

clue.text: Issue direction to many a nation

annotationWithheld.why: Issue direction to many a nation: E (direction) leaves MANATION, which 'many a nation' gives only by dropping Y, A, N with no clue word signalling it
annotationWithheld.clue: Issue direction to many a nation

clue.text: A capital leaf

parts.note: a leaf carved on the top of a classical column, a capital

explanation.surface: An excellent leaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like 'excellent' but is the head of a column: Corinthian capitals are carved with this plant's leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant's leaves are the motif carved on Corinthian column heads.

clue.text: Unit usage makes a good man

indicators.note: the words Unit usage are made into something else, rearranged

explanation.surface: A unit's customs produce a fine fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'good man' is a saint: Augustine of Hippo, or of Canterbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Augustine is a holy figure, and saints are the crossword's good men.

clue.text: The face of Dickens?

parts.note: an old slang word for the face, which was also the pen-name of Dickens's illustrator

explanation.surface: What did Dickens look like?
explanation.walkthrough: Hablot K. Browne illustrated Dickens under a pen-name that is old slang for the face (from physiognomy).
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for the visage, short for physiognomy, and the signature of the novelist's illustrator.

clue.text: Flavour without stint and with enjoyment

parts.note: zest is a piquant flavour
fully means completely, without holding back

explanation.surface: Flavour applied generously and relished.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something zestfully means doing it with gusto and relish.

clue.text: Making short work of a barrister?

definitions.text: Making short work of a barrister?

parts.words: Making short work of a barrister?
parts.note: giving a lawyer his instructions, a brief being both short and a lawyer's case

explanation.surface: Dealing quickly with a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: A solicitor instructs a barrister by handing over a brief; 'brief' also means short.
explanation.definitionFit: Instructing counsel is done with a brief, and brief also means short.

clue.text: Short paragraphs fail to worry the guileless knight

parts.note: pars is the journalists' shortening of paragraphs

indicators.note: to worry a word is to shake it about, so the letters of fail are rearranged

explanation.surface: Brief items in the press fail to trouble an innocent knight.
explanation.walkthrough: PARS (short for paragraphs) is followed by IFAL, from 'fail' with 'to worry' as anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagner's Arthurian hero is the pure fool, innocent of guile, who finds the Grail.

clue.text: Makes cosy jackets for those inside

definitions.meaning: insulates, as pipes or tanks are wrapped against the cold
old convicts serving time in prison

explanation.surface: Someone knits warm coats for the people indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: To insulate a boiler is to lag it; old convicts are lags.

clue.text: Rock in this state doesn't amount to much

definitions.text: Rock in this state doesn't amount to much

parts.words: Rock in this state doesn't amount to much
parts.note: the state capital is Little Rock, so the rock there is small

explanation.surface: Geologically, the state is unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital of this US state is Little Rock: a rock that doesn't amount to much.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern US state has Little Rock as its capital city.

clue.text: Like the Wedding-Guest the morning after

definitions.text: Like the Wedding-Guest the morning after

parts.words: Like the Wedding-Guest the morning after
parts.note: Coleridge's Ancient Mariner ends with the Wedding-Guest rising the next morning more sorrowful and wiser

explanation.surface: A hungover wedding guest the next day.
explanation.walkthrough: The end of Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner: 'A sadder and a wiser man, / He rose the morrow morn.'
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's guest woke more sorrowful and wiser after hearing the Mariner's tale.

clue.text: Old hand reading Greats perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the word Greats could take another form, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An experienced student studying classics at Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: Greats is Oxford's classics degree, so the surface suggests a student; 'perhaps' is the anagram signal, 'reading' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An old stager is a veteran, someone long experienced.

clue.text: Keep governor in Cornwall?

parts.note: the boss of a castle, read as the name of a coastal village in Cornwall

explanation.surface: Retain a governor in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' is a castle stronghold, and its governor its boss; the Cornish village name reads as 'boss castle'.
explanation.definitionFit: The harbour village on Cornwall's north coast sounds like a castle's boss.

clue.text: Foundation for a "sweet girl-graduate"?

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a graduate
sis, short for sister, is a girl

explanation.surface: Make-up for Tennyson's sweet girl-graduate.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's The Princess speaks of 'sweet girl-graduates'; read as a BA who is a SIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A basis is the groundwork on which something rests.

clue.text: But nothing corny about these arrows

definitions.text: But nothing corny about these arrows

parts.words: But nothing corny about these arrows
parts.note: a bundle of arrows takes the name usually given to bound stalks of corn

explanation.surface: Arrows that are not trite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corny' looks like 'trite', but it means of corn: a bundle of arrows has the same name as a bound bundle of corn.
explanation.definitionFit: A bundle of arrows, like reaped stalks tied together, is called by the same collective noun.

clue.text: Bearer of berries in church

definitions.meaning: the shrub Sambucus, with dark berries
a lay officer in a Presbyterian church

explanation.surface: A berry-bearing plant growing inside a church.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sambucus shrub bears clusters of berries; a lay official of a church has the same name.

clue.text: A poke in the lower leg causes a row

parts.note: the shin is the front of the lower leg
a dig is a poke

explanation.surface: Kicking someone in the leg starts a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: A row here is a noisy party or commotion, not a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A shindig is a noisy party or a disturbance, a rumpus.

clue.text: " And much as Wine has play'd the "(Fitzgerald)

definitions.text: " And much as Wine has play'd the "(Fitzgerald)

parts.words: " And much as Wine has play'd the "(Fitzgerald)
parts.note: a quotation from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, where wine has acted as an unbeliever

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from FitzGerald's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rubaiyat line runs 'And much as Wine has play'd the Infidel', the missing word being the unbeliever.
explanation.definitionFit: The verse casts wine as an unbeliever who has betrayed the poet.

clue.text: What a hulk Tom Bowling was

definitions.text: What a hulk Tom Bowling was

parts.words: What a hulk Tom Bowling was
parts.note: Dibdin's sea song begins 'Here, a ... hulk, lies poor Tom Bowling'

explanation.surface: Tom Bowling was a big man.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Dibdin's song 'Tom Bowling' opens 'Here, a sheer hulk, lies poor Tom Bowling', a hulk being a dismasted ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A dismasted ship is a mere hulk; the song calls the dead sailor an utter one.

clue.text: Just like clockwork

parts.note: happening at even, predictable intervals

explanation.surface: Everything going smoothly.
explanation.definitionFit: Clockwork ticks at even intervals, so its rhythm is steady and periodic.
